transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-01 16:00 PT
Duration: ~44 minutes
Attendees: Priya Shah (Redwood AE), Evan Morales (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (CTO, SableWorks), Roberto Diaz (Lead ML Eng), Ellie Park (Head of Security), Tom Howard (Product Manager)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on unit economics and which hosting mode makes sense given SableWorks' budget ceilings and latency goals. Discussed per-token cost sensitivity, batching/prefix cache levers, dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, and security requirements (KMS, audit logs). Agreed to run a short benchmark and exchange a basic cost-model spreadsheet.

Topics covered: per-token pricing, batching and KV/prefix cache, throughput targets, burst capacity, residency/VPC, SOC2/KMS, pilot scope

Transcript body:
[00:00] Priya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I think we've got about 45 minutes, we'll run through a quick intake on budget and usage then Evan will go into some of the technical levers, sound good?
[00:12] Maya: Yep, that's perfect. We're mainly trying to understand whether Redwood hosted is viable or if we need to go dedicated/private right away. Budget is pretty tight for FY27.
[00:20] Priya: Great, high level first — can you give us current numbers? Requests per second, average tokens per request, and any latency SLOs?
[00:28] Roberto: Sure. For the pilot we'll be at roughly 200 requests per minute initially, target is maybe 1,000/min in production. Average tokens per request is around 140 tokens. Tail latency target is 95th under 300ms for the user-facing flows.
[00:46] Evan: 95th under 300ms at 140 tokens is ambitious on some backends but doable with correct provisioning and batching choices. Quick clarifying Q — are these real-time chat-like calls or batch scoring?
[00:58] Tom: Mostly chat-like, interactive. Some async scoring for background workflows but the user experiences need the low latency.
[01:08] Priya: Ok, so latency matters. Budgetwise what's your ceiling? rough monthly spend?
[01:15] Maya: We have a run-rate target of about $25k/month for inference costs initially. Can be flexible if we can prove ROI but the finance team is strict.
[01:25] Priya: That's helpful. We typically show customers how per-token pricing + batching can change unit economics by orders of magnitude. Evan, want to walk through the levers?
[01:34] Evan: Yeah. At a high level there are three levers that move cost per inference: sequence length (tokens), batching, and caching. Also model family and quantization — smaller, quantized variants can cut GPU cycles. For chat at 140 tokens, continuous batching can help but there's a latency tradeoff.
[01:50] Roberto: Can you explain continuous batching? I saw that term in the docs but not sure how it affects tail latency.
[01:56] Evan: Sure — continuous batching collects concurrent requests into micro-batches to improve GPU utilization. Instead of firing a separate kernel per request, it packs them. That reduces per-token cost but if you wait too long to batch you'll add queueing latency. We have policy knobs: max batching latency, preferred batch size, and SLO-aware routing so latency-sensitive traffic can bypass larger batch windows.
[02:20] Maya: Ok so we could choose tighter batch windows for UI flows and looser for background jobs.
[02:25] Evan: Exactly. Also prefix/KV cache is huge for chatbots where users ask similar prompts or there's a shared system prompt — caching earlier KV states avoids recomputing the entire context. Some customers call it prefix cache, some say KV cash (laugh) — transcription errors for sure.
[02:40] Ellie: On caching, we need to understand residency — what data persists in cache and where. If KV cache lives on the GPU host, is that data encrypted and under our KMS control?
[02:51] Evan: On Redwood Private and Dedicated we can integrate with your KMS so keys are customer-managed. For hosted, we support envelope encryption and can provide per-tenant keys in many cases; we should map that out. Cache contents are ephemeral for inference but they could contain user tokens. We recommend encrypting at-rest and restricting admin access.
[03:10] Priya: Also worth noting Redwood has burst capacity options if you need to handle spikes without paying for full reserved clusters — that's often a decider for teams balancing cost.
[03:20] Maya: The finance team asked: how do we estimate per-1M tokens cost? We need a simple model we can show execs.
[03:27] Priya: We'll send a baseline model. Rough example off top of head: hosted per-1M tokens for a standard LLM variant might be X — sorry can't quote exact public numbers in this call — but the spreadsheet will let you plug tokens per request, requests per minute, and we show Hosted vs Dedicated amortized GPU cost including reserved capacity math, plus savings from batching and quantization.
[03:50] Tom: I want concrete examples. If we target 1M tokens per day at 140 tokens per request, how would that look?
[03:58] Evan: Let's ballpark. 1M tokens/day / 140 tokens = ~7,100 requests/day. If evenly spread that's ~5 requests/minute — but you get spikes. The key is the per-token GPU seconds. With batching and a quantized model we may be able to reduce GPU time per token by 30-50% compared to naive runs.
[04:19] Roberto: Is there an easy way to see where caching helps? For example, we have a handful of prompts reused across users.
[04:24] Evan: Yes — in the model of cost, we separate cached prefix tokens vs fresh tokens. If a 40-token system prompt is cached you only pay for the new 100 tokens. With per-token billing that maps nicely to cost savings. Also Redwood Optimize suggests cache-friendly prompt templates.
[04:40] Ellie: Security follow-up — audit logs, RBAC, and SAML are non-negotiable for us. For Private we assume we get more control. How mature are Redwood's audit logs for per-request traceability?
[04:51] Priya: We have per-request tracing, token-level cost breakdown, and can export logs to your SIEM. For Private deployments you can keep logs on-prem. We'll include the SOC2 summary and log retention options in the packet.
[05:03] Maya: Another question — for dedicated, what's the minimum committed capacity? Finance worries about stranded GPU costs if utilization is low.
[05:12] Priya: Dedicated typically has monthly reserved pools; minimum depends on the GPU type — for smaller pilots we often recommend a small reserved pool plus burst-to-hosted to absorb spikes. That reduces stranded cost. We'll detail typical commit sizes in the spreadsheet.
[05:26] Tom: Any caveats on model versions? If we roll a new policy model and latency worsens, can we fall back to a cheaper variant automatically?
[05:33] Evan: Yes — Redwood supports routing policies and automatic fallback to compatible model variants based on latency or error budgets. It's how we keep SLAs while minimizing cost.
[05:43] Roberto: Ok, what about quantization? How aggressive can we be without degrading output quality? We've seen hallucination increase with 4-bit in some tasks.
[05:51] Evan: Totally — quantization tradeoff is model and task dependent. We run evals on your prompt set during the pilot. Often 8-bit or mixed quant works well; 4-bit can be fine for some families but we validate. Redwood Optimize will recommend a quant profile.
[06:07] Maya: On timeline — we want to present a pilot proposal to finance next Tuesday morning. Can we get numbers and a proposed benchmark run by Friday?
[06:15] Priya: Yes — we'll aim for a Friday deliverable. Evan will capture the sample prompt set and test plan.
[06:20] Ellie: For the security packet, please include network diagrams showing where keys live and how logs flow. We need that for procurement.
[06:27] Priya: Noted. We'll include a high-level data flow and a list of controls.
[06:31] Maya: What would success look like for the pilot? Low cost per active user, latency under 300ms 95th, and no security blockers.
[06:39] Priya: Great — we'll make that the pilot KPIs.
[06:42] Tom: A few nitty-gritty things — our peak concurrency window is 1k concurrent users for 15 minutes, then it drops. So burst capacity matters.
[06:51] Evan: For 1k concurrency we might avoid a naive hosted-only approach. Dedicated with burst-to-hosted or overprovisioned dedicated nodes with autoscale policies would be safer. We'll size that in the cost model.
[07:03] Roberto: Also, we run a small reranker step for top-K scoring after generation. How does that factor in cost? Two model calls per request effectively double tokens.
[07:11] Evan: Exactly — the cost model needs to include multi-step pipelines. If rerank is a smaller dense model you can often run that on CPU or smaller GPUs to save. We'll capture pipeline steps in the spreadsheet.
[07:23] Maya: Anything else from Redwood?
[07:26] Priya: Just to confirm next actions: we'll send the pricing + spreadsheet, Evan will propose a benchmark, and Ellie will send the security questions. Also we'll set up a 60-minute benchmark session next week.
[07:38] Ellie: I'll compile questions today.
[07:40] Tom: We'll get you a sample prompt set and real traffic shape by Thursday.
[07:45] Priya: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet.
